newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia threatens tax debtors with bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia threatens tax debtors with bankruptcy.

text.p: The Russian government has threatened several big companies with bankruptcy in its latest and toughest effort to clamp down on massive tax avoidance.

Pyotr Mostovoi, head of the state bankruptcy agency, told a news conference on Tuesday that the government would start bankruptcy proceedings against six big firms unless they paid overdue taxes within a week.
The firms include oil giants AO Tatneft and AO Purneftegaz as well as truck maker AO KamAZ, based in the ethnic republic of Tatarstan.
Mostovoi said a commission of tax experts had decided the six firms were profitable and fully capable of paying the money they owed the government.

"We cannot allow our most profitable companies to break the laws of God and society," he said. "The debts make fractions of a percent of these companies' turnovers and none of them can say it is incapable of paying."

Tax arrears, part of a cycle of non-payments throughout Russia, are one of Russia's most pressing economic problems. President Boris Yeltsin last week announced the creation of an emergency commission to work out how to resolve the problem.

"I know taxes are high in Russia today, but we will be able to lower them only if we manage to ensure compliance with tax legislation," said Yeltsin, who faces an operation in the next two months to improve the blood supply to his heart.
"First we collect taxes and then we will cut them."
Mostovoi said other companies facing the threat of bankruptcy proceedings were carmaker AO Moskvich, alumina company AO Achinsky Glinozemny Zavod and oil refinery AO Krasnodarnefteorgsintez.
He said each company had paid less than 10 percent of their 1996 taxes in the first half of the year. They owed the government a total of more than 1.5 trillion roubles ($275.7 million).
The government was now examining the financial situation at 10 more companies, he said.

The shortfall in tax collection has left government coffers short of funds to tackle social problems and worried the International Monetary Fund, which sees fulfilment of Russia's tough 1996 budget as the key to releasing monthly tranches of a three-year $10 billion loan.
The government failed to receive more than 50 trillion roubles in planned tax revenue in the first eight months of this year, the commission said in a statement.

Mostovoi said some 185 of Russia's biggest companies were responsible for a large share of the debt. Gazprom GAZP.RTS, the world's biggest gas company, acknowledges it owes more than 15 trillion roubles in taxes.
But the monopoly gas producer says it is owed more than three times that amount by consumers, including the government.
Mostovoi praised other companies for paying their debts on time despite financial problems.

He said that many Russian companies used cash to pay suppliers and creditors rather than paying taxes or wages. The shortfall caused massive wage arrears for government sector workers and left pensioners without their pensions.
Social policy chief Viktor Ilyushin said on Monday that a quarter of Russians were living below subsistence levels and complained he had little power or money to put things right.

"However deplorable it is, we have to acknowledge that mass poverty has arisen and the number of citizens with incomes below the subsistence minimum is a quarter of the whole population of Russia," he told a news conference. ($1=5440 Rouble)
